cards.title: Sublinear communication for perfectly secure two-party computation
cards.area: Cryptography
cards.formal: Is there a uniform two-party protocol in the trusted correlated-randomness model that perfectly computes every Boolean circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\times\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) with polynomial setup and computation, and online communication \(O(n+g(s))\) for some function \(g(s)=o(s)\), where \(s\) is the circuit's supplied size? More precisely, seek fixed algorithms, constants \(K,q\ge1\), and \(g:\mathbb N_{\ge1}\to\mathbb R_{\ge1}\) with \(\lim_{s\to\infty}g(s)/s=0\), such that every circuit and every pair of inputs satisfy the correctness and privacy conditions below; dealer computation, total setup length and both parties' computation are at most \(K(n+s+1)^q\), while at most \(K(n+g(s))\) bits are exchanged online. The circuit is arbitrary, without a layering or depth restriction. The additive input-length term fixes the source's sublinearity question in a form that also covers circuits of linear size.

sentences: Two parties want to compute a Boolean circuit while keeping each input perfectly private.
A trusted dealer can distribute correlated randomness before either input is supplied.
The question asks whether polynomial setup and computation can give online communication sublinear in the circuit size, apart from the input-length cost.
Such savings are known for layered circuits, while completely optimal communication can require exponential setup.
The unresolved target covers arbitrary circuits with perfect passive privacy and shared outputs.

cards.definitions:
A circuit is an explicitly given finite directed acyclic graph with \(2n\) input vertices, Boolean constants, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one designated output. Fan-out is unrestricted. Let \(s\) count all vertices, including inputs and constants; in particular \(s\ge2n\). Gates and predecessors are encoded in topological order with binary indices. Both parties and the dealer know this public description. The inputs \(x_0,x_1\in\{0,1\}^n\) are private to their respective parties. The size in the bound is that of the supplied circuit; the protocol may optimize its computation, but cannot charge an artificially padded circuit to increase its communication allowance.

Before the parties receive their inputs, a trusted randomized dealer, given only \(C\), samples finite correlated strings \((r_0,r_1)\) and privately sends \(r_b\) to party \(b\). These strings may depend on \(C\) but not on either input. The dealer then takes no further part. Dealer randomness consists of independent fair bits; its computation and output length obey the polynomial bound on every run. Independent local random tapes can be included in these strings. After this phase the parties are deterministic machines on their input, setup string and message history. Their descriptions are fixed across all circuits and lengths, and their complete online runtimes obey the same polynomial bound. There is no other setup, oracle or computational hardness assumption.

The parties exchange binary messages and output private bits \(y_0,y_1\). Perfect correctness means
\[\Pr[y_0\mathbin\oplus y_1=C(x_0,x_1)]=1\]
for every input pair, where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. The task uses the source's shared-output convention: neither party is required to learn the reconstructed answer. Perfect privacy against one passive corruption means that, for each \(b\) and each fixed \(C,x_b\), the distribution of party \(b\)'s entire view is identical for every choice of the other party's input. Its view includes \(r_b\), all sent and received messages and its output. A passive adversary follows the protocol and may inspect that entire view with unlimited computation; the parties do not collude. Privacy and correctness have zero error.

Online cost is the worst-case number of bits sent in both directions, over inputs and all dealer outcomes of positive probability. Message boundaries, control information and input-dependent stopping must be encoded in this communication; timing and silence are not free channels. There is no separate round bound beyond polynomial runtime. The dealer's private deliveries are excluded from online communication but included in the setup-length bound. For every family whose circuit size is polynomial in \(n\), the stated \(\operatorname{poly}(n+s)\) resource bound is polynomial in the input length, as required by the source. A single choice of algorithms, \(K,q,g\) must work for all such families, not only a fixed function or depth.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence, including perfect privacy, correctness, polynomial setup/computation and a uniform sublinear \(g\), or prove that no such protocol and resource bounds exist. A protocol for layered circuits only, a computationally secure construction, or a truth-table protocol using setup exponential in \(n\) does not settle this target. A negative answer must rule out all sublinear savings allowed above, rather than only exactly optimal or one-round online communication.

context_blocks.text: The input-independent setup is a resource, not a free truth table of the function. Beaver-style evaluation uses linear-size correlated randomness and linear online communication. A one-time truth table can make communication linear in the input length, but its exponential setup falls outside this question.

Couteau gives perfect passive-security protocols for layered circuits with communication \(O(n+s/\log\log s)\) for a fixed number of parties and a constant-size output, using polynomial storage. In a layered circuit every edge joins consecutive layers. Transforming a general circuit into this form can increase its size and therefore does not automatically give sublinear cost relative to the original circuit.

The 2023 source proves exponential setup lower bounds when each party sends exactly as much information as its input, including a stronger bound for a single online round. Its functions have a two-bit shared output and input domain size \(N\); the lower bounds are in \(N\), which is exponential in input bit length. These endpoint results do not rule out \(O(n+g(s))\) communication with additional interaction.

Computationally secure protocols may replace large correlations by short pseudorandom descriptions under hardness assumptions. Perfect privacy here requires exact equality of view distributions even for an unbounded observer, so those constructions answer a different question.

cards.title: Polynomial-time computationally sound verification of \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\)
cards.area: Cryptography
cards.formal: Do there exist deterministic uniform algorithms \(P,V\), integers \(C>c\ge1\), and a constant \(K\ge2\) giving the following plain-model argument system for exact \(\#\mathrm{SAT}\), without unproved hardness assumptions? On a Boolean formula \(\Phi\) encoded in \(N\) bits, \(P\) produces a proof of length at most \((N+1)^C\) in time \(T_P(N)=2^{K(N+1)^c}\). The verifier runs in time \(K(N+1)^C\) and outputs either the exact number of satisfying assignments or the rejection symbol \(\bot\). Completeness requires \(V(\Phi,P(\Phi))=\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) on every valid formula. Soundness requires that every uniform randomized adversary running in any fixed polynomial in \(T_P(N)\) has only negligible probability, as a function of \(T_P(N)\), of generating a length-\(N\) formula and a proof on which \(V\) outputs an incorrect number. This card fixes the unconditional version of the source question; conditional constructions are recorded below.
cards.why: Exact counting requires certifying that no satisfying assignments were missed, as well as that counted assignments exist. This question tests whether computational soundness can give deterministic short verification of such global information while retaining an honest prover with a specified running time. It connects the power of proof systems with derandomization and the distinction between uniform computational attacks and arbitrary false witnesses.
cards.status_note: Open Problem 4.5 of the 2023 source was checked together with the 3 April 2025 revision of Chen–Rothblum–Tell on 2026-09-14. The latter gives conditional polynomial-time verification under strong hardness assumptions; this card explicitly selects unconditional existence with its honest-prover/adversary convention. A bounded later-work search found no unconditional resolution.

sentences: The task is to check the exact number of satisfying assignments to a Boolean formula in polynomial time.
An exponential-time honest prover supplies a short proof to a fully deterministic verifier.
Even adversaries running in any polynomial in the honest prover’s time must almost never find a false counting claim that the verifier accepts.
A 2025 theorem gives such verification for polynomial-space claims under strong hardness assumptions.
This card asks whether the specified counting-verification system exists without those unproved assumptions.

cards.definitions:
Fix a polynomial-time parsable binary encoding of formulas over AND, OR and NOT. An instance lists its \(n\) variables explicitly, so \(n\le N\), and its formula is a finite tree with leaves among those variables and Boolean constants. The value \(\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi)\) is the number of assignments in \(\{0,1\}^n\) on which the formula evaluates to one, including choices of any listed unused variables. The answer is written in binary and has at most \(n+1\) bits. Measuring resources in the full encoding length fixes the meaning of polynomial-size formulas and includes the cost of reading their descriptions.

The prover and verifier are deterministic multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. The proof is one finite binary string; there is no interaction, oracle, common reference string, advice, secret setup or verifier randomness. The verifier rejects malformed instances and overlong proofs. It halts within its stated bound on every input, reading at most one symbol beyond the permitted proof length to detect excess input. Increasing the fixed constant \(K\) absorbs encoding and rejection overhead. The honest prover must construct its proof in the stated exponential time; mere existence of a proof with no bound on its production is insufficient.

More explicitly, for every uniform probabilistic Turing machine \(A\) whose worst-case runtime on \(1^N\) is at most \(T_P(N)^a\) for some fixed \(a\ge1\), and for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(N_{A,d}\) such that, for every \(N\ge N_{A,d}\),
\[\Pr_{(\Phi,\pi)\leftarrow A(1^N)}\bigl[\Phi\text{ is valid},\ |\Phi|=N,\ V(\Phi,\pi)\notin\{\#\mathrm{SAT}(\Phi),\bot\}\bigr]\le T_P(N)^{-d}.\]
Probability is over independent fair random bits used by \(A\). Any output that is not a valid formula/proof pair is a failed attack. The adversary chooses both the formula and its proof, knows \(P,V\), and has no nonuniform advice or auxiliary input. The polynomial exponent \(a\) may be arbitrarily large and is not fixed by the protocol. Negligibility is measured in the honest prover's time, rather than merely inverse polynomial in the formula length. The constants \(c,C,K\) and the two machines must be fixed before quantifying over adversaries and accuracy exponents.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a system exists, including all completeness, uniformity, running-time and soundness requirements, or prove that no such system exists. A positive answer must be unconditional. A construction assuming a conjectured hard function is progress but does not settle this selected version. Randomized verification, interaction, a setup string, soundness only against polynomial-in-input-length adversaries, or an unbounded honest prover changes the question.

context_blocks.text: Computational soundness permits incorrect proofs to exist, provided no adversary with the specified resources can generate a false instance together with an accepted proof. Ordinary NP soundness forbids every false proof. Allowing nonuniform advice would let an adversary hardwire a false pair at each input length, removing this distinction.

The honest prover is allowed exponential time, and the adversary is allowed every polynomial in that time. Requiring a polynomial-time honest prover would instead give a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm by composing prover and verifier. Allowing an arbitrarily stronger honest prover than the attacker would also distort the model; the later paper explains why.

The 2023 source gives, under strong assumptions, verification in time \(2^{\varepsilon n}\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), with an honest prover and adversaries using \(2^{O(n)}\) time. Its next question asks for a polynomial-time verifier.

The 2025 paper proves \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\subseteq\mathrm{cs}\text{-}\mathrm{NP}\) under strong assumptions about functions that remain hard for small-space computation on efficiently samplable inputs. Its Definition 1.1 explicitly allows a polynomial-time verifier with an exponential-time honest prover. Applying its polynomial-space verification result to exact-count claims gives conditional progress on this card, since exact counting can be performed in polynomial space. The paper does not prove the required hardness assumptions.

cards.definitions:
The common input is the full truth table \(x\) of a function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), with \(n\geq1\) and \(N=2^n\). Let \(C(f)\) be its minimum Boolean circuit size. Fix the standard basis of binary AND and OR and unary NOT, with constant inputs available, arbitrary fan-out, one output, and size equal to the number of gates. Circuits are acyclic and compute every truth-table entry correctly.

A yes-instance satisfies \(C(f)\leq N^\varepsilon\). A no-instance satisfies \(C(f)>N^{1-\varepsilon}\). Inputs between these thresholds have no required decision outcome. The strict no-threshold follows the formal definition in the later source; the thresholds need not be integers. The constant \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, not supplied per instance. The task has both low-complexity and high-complexity promised inputs at arbitrarily large lengths.

An interactive proof has an honest prover \(P\) and a randomized verifier \(V\). Total communication, rounds and verifier computation are polynomial in \(N\), the explicit truth-table length. No computational bound is imposed on the prover. On every yes-instance, the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(2/3\). On every no-instance, every cheating prover, including an unbounded one, causes acceptance with probability at most \(1/3\). This is a proof system; soundness only against efficient provers would be an argument system.

Computational zero knowledge requires that for every randomized polynomial-time verifier \(V^*\), including one given arbitrary polynomial-length auxiliary information \(z\), there is a randomized polynomial-time simulator \(S_{V^*}\). Given only \(x,z\), it produces a distribution computationally indistinguishable from the entire view of \(V^*\) in the honest-prover interaction on \(x\). That view includes the common input, auxiliary information, verifier randomness, messages and final output. The simulator is not given a small circuit or other witness.

Indistinguishability is required on all yes-instances: every polynomial-size distinguishing circuit has only negligible advantage in \(N\), uniformly over these instances and polynomial-length auxiliary strings. Negligible means smaller than \(N^{-c}\) for every fixed positive \(c\) at sufficiently large \(N\). The simulator and verifier use the ordinary polynomial-time convention of the later source. No setup, random oracle, trusted third party or hardness assumption is supplied.

The chosen circuit basis fixes a concrete representation. The existential constant-gap formulation tolerates constant-factor changes of standard finite bases by choosing a slightly wider gap and handling finitely many small lengths separately. It does not identify circuits with a shortest program: MINKT instead bounds the program length needed to print a string within a supplied time budget, and its gap parameters constitute a separate choice.

The target asks for one protocol meeting worst-case completeness, soundness and zero knowledge at every input length. A protocol that succeeds on most inputs from a particular distribution or only at infinitely many lengths is a weaker result.
cards.answer_criterion: Give some fixed admissible gap constant and a protocol with proofs of polynomial verifier and simulator cost, completeness, soundness against all provers, and computational zero knowledge against arbitrary efficient auxiliary-input verifiers, without assuming one-way functions or another hardness premise. A negative answer must rule out the specified protocols for every constant in this selected gap family. Failure for that family would not by itself refute all alternatives in the original broader question.

cards.area: Proof complexity
cards.formal:
Does the following implication hold?
\[\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{Frege is not polynomially bounded}.\]
Precisely, assuming that some NP language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuit family, must it be true that for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every constant \(C\ge1\), there is a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) such that every Frege proof \(\pi\) of \(\varphi\), in the fixed system below, has
\[|\pi|>C(|\varphi|+1)^k?\]
This asks for a conditional connection between two lower-bound statements. It does not separately require proving the circuit-hardness premise.
cards.why: General Boolean circuit lower bounds and Frege proof lower bounds are two major barriers in complexity theory. A positive implication would make progress on the former sufficient for the latter, even without an explicit hard-tautology construction. It would clarify whether these difficulties are formally linked or whether proof complexity requires an additional source of hardness.

cards.definitions:
A language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) is in NP if there are a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine \(V\) and a polynomial \(p\) such that \(x\in L\) exactly when some binary string \(y\), with \(|y|\le p(|x|)\), satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). A Boolean circuit has input bits, constants zero and one, fan-in-two AND/OR gates, NOT gates, and one output. Its size is its number of gates, and its depth and fan-out are unrestricted. The class P/poly consists of languages decided at each input length \(n\) by a circuit \(D_n\) of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\), for fixed \(C,k\). These circuits need not be produced by an algorithm: they may be chosen nonuniformly. Thus NP not contained in P/poly asserts that at least one NP language has no such circuit family.

Fix the following classical Hilbert presentation of Frege. Formulas are finite trees built from propositional variables \(p_0,p_1,\ldots\), negation \(\neg\), and implication \(\to\). Under a Boolean assignment, negation reverses the truth value and \(A\to B\) is false exactly when \(A\) is true and \(B\) false. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its finitely many variables. The axiom schemes, allowing arbitrary formulas \(A,B,D\), are
\[A\to(B\to A),\]
\[(A\to(B\to D))\to((A\to B)\to(A\to D)),\]
\[(\neg A\to\neg B)\to(B\to A).\]
The only inference rule is modus ponens: from earlier lines \(A\) and \(A\to B\), infer \(B\). A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each an instance of an axiom scheme or obtained by this rule; its last formula is the theorem proved. No extension axioms introducing a new variable as an abbreviation for a formula are allowed.

Choose a fixed uniquely parsable binary tree encoding with constant-length tags for connectives and binary, self-delimited variable indices. Let \(|\varphi|\) be its bit length. Encode a proof by its full sequence of formula strings, with line delimiters; let \(|\pi|\) be that total bit length. Identical subformulas are written out each time they occur, not stored as a shared circuit. Earlier proof lines may be reused in multiple inferences. Including explicit rule tags and premise indices changes these sizes by at most polynomial factors and does not affect polynomial boundedness. The source recalls that standard finite complete Frege presentations polynomially simulate one another, so fixing this presentation does not change its lower-bound question.

Frege is polynomially bounded if there exist \(C,k\) such that every tautology has at least one proof of size at most \(C(|\varphi|+1)^k\). Its negation does not require a polynomial-time generator for the hard tautologies or a single explicit family: existence of arbitrarily hard tautologies with the displayed quantifiers suffices. Formula size, proof size and circuit-input length are different parameters and are not silently identified.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed implication or of its negation. A positive proof may use exactly the circuit-hardness premise, without assuming additional cryptographic hardness, a feasible-interpolation property of Frege, or a lower bound for another system. A proof of the negation must establish both NP not contained in P/poly and polynomial boundedness of the fixed Frege system. An oracle separation or an obstruction to one reduction technique is not itself a negation of the stated unrelativized implication.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to \{0,1\}\), on arbitrary nonempty finite sets X,Y, satisfies $D(f)\le C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k$, where \(r(f)\) is the real rank of its \(0/1\) communication matrix and \(D(f)\) is its deterministic communication complexity?
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know the complete function f and the protocol. They exchange bits interactively; each next transmitted bit is a deterministic function of the sender’s own input and the previous transcript. A binary protocol tree specifies whose turn it is, and every leaf has a Boolean output that must equal \(f(x,y)\) for every input pair reaching it. \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such exact protocols, of the maximum number of transmitted bits on an input pair. The number of rounds and the local computation are unrestricted; protocol description length is not charged. The communication matrix \(M_{f}\) has rows X, columns Y, and entry \(f(x,y); r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{R}(M_{f})\) is ordinary matrix rank over the real numbers. The +2 makes the statement unambiguous for rank zero or one. The same constants C,k must work for all matrix dimensions and all functions. There are no undefined entries, input promises, random bits, quantum messages, approximation errors, or restrictions to one-way protocols. Sign rank and approximate rank are different parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

Sudakov and Tomon improve the universal upper bound to \(O(\sqrt{r})\). The 2023 preprint is published online in 2024 and in Mathematical Programming volume 212 in 2025.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint revisits the construction without first converting its pointer alphabet to Boolean bits and reports a more precise lower bound \(\Omega ((\log  r)^{2}/\log  \log  r)\). This still has a fixed polynomial exponent and therefore supports no refutation of log-rank.

A recent equivalent formulation isolates the role of cancellation more sharply. Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley show that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r \log  r)\) rectangle indicator matrices. The open task can then be expressed as converting such signed decompositions into positive disjoint rectangle decompositions with quasipolynomial growth. This theorem supplies a new formulation, while the needed conversion remains unresolved.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, H(f)\le C I(f)\), where \(H(f)\) is the base-two Shannon entropy of its squared Fourier coefficients and \(I(f)\) is its total influence under the uniform distribution, as defined below?
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq [n]\), let \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and let \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Put \(q_{S}=\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\); Parseval gives \(\sum _{S} q_{S}=1\). Define \(H(f)=\sum _{S} q_{S} \log _{2}(1/q_{S})\), with a zero summand when \(q_{S}=0\). If x is uniform and \(x^{\oplus i}\) differs only by flipping coordinate i, define \(I_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})]\) and \(I(f)=\sum _{i=1}^{n} I_{i}(f)=\sum _{S} |S|q_{S}\). All Boolean functions are quantified, without circuit-size, monotonicity, balance, or efficient-computability assumptions. The same C must work for all dimensions and all functions. Constant functions have \(H(f)=I(f)=0\) and satisfy the non-strict inequality.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 primary paper explicitly retains classical FEI as open and proves only specified classes. The August 2026 disproof is of the quantum extension. No classical resolution was found in the checked sources; the formulation uses Shannon entropy, uniform measure and scalar Boolean functions throughout.

context_blocks.text: The Fourier expansion expresses a Boolean rule as a linear combination of parity tests on subsets of its inputs. Squaring the coefficients produces a probability distribution on these subsets. Its entropy measures how dispersed that distribution is; total influence measures the expected size of a subset sampled from it. The conjecture says that the Boolean constraint forces the first quantity to be at most a constant times the second, even though there are exponentially many possible subsets.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

A useful consequence would be spectral concentration: for any \(0<\delta <1\), all but \(\delta\) of the Fourier mass could be captured by at most \(2^{C I(f)/\delta}\) coefficients. This follows by applying Markov’s inequality to the surprisal \(\log _{2}(1/q_{S})\) of a random spectral subset. It supplies a quantitative connection between stability under individual bit flips and approximation by a short linear combination of parities. The dependence on \(\delta\) is essential; the claim is not an accuracy-independent support bound.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou establish the conjecture for symmetric Boolean functions and for functions computed by read-once decision trees. Their paper also explains the connection to learning DNF formulas: the conjecture would imply polynomial Fourier concentration for a DNF with polynomially many terms, at each fixed approximation accuracy. This is a structural learning-theory consequence, rather than an assertion that arbitrary Boolean functions become efficiently learnable.

A general bound proved by Han is \(H(f)\le O(I(f)+\sum _{i} I_{i}(f) \log (1/I_{i}(f)))\). The extra term records how influence is distributed across coordinates. It can exceed a constant multiple of \(I(f)\), so this does not settle the conjecture. The December 2025 revision adds an acknowledgement of related earlier work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. Bounds on min-entropy concern the largest Fourier coefficient alone and must not be substituted for a Shannon-entropy bound.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s June 2026 revision verifies additional classes, including \(\delta\)-tribes and functions with specified separation properties. Their method splits on selected coordinates and stops at restrictions already satisfying FEI. It also demonstrates failure of a stronger sufficient inequality when the splitting coordinate is chosen badly. Those examples do satisfy FEI when handled with a suitable coordinate, so they expose a limitation of that inductive route rather than a counterexample to the conjecture.

Slote’s August 2026 preprint disproves a quantum analogue using Hermitian unitary operators with flat, very large Pauli expansions. For the constructed degree-d operators, the spectral entropy grows quadratically in d while the influence grows linearly. These are quantum Boolean functions, not scalar maps on the classical Boolean cube. The result makes the distinction between the two settings concrete and does not provide a classical counterexample.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C\ge 1\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\) and every real multilinear polynomial f of degree at most d satisfying \(0\le f(x)\le 1\) for every \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\), some coordinate i satisfies \(Inf_{i}(f)\ge (\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\)?
cards.definitions: All expectations use the uniform distribution on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\). Write \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq [n]} \hat\{f\}(S)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}\), with \(\hat\{f\}(S)=E_{x}[f(x)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}]\); degree at most d means \(\hat\{f\}(S)=0\) when |\(S|>d\). Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be x with just coordinate i negated. Define \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=E[(f- E f)^{2}]=\sum_{S\ne \varnothing}\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\) and \(Inf_{i}(f)=E[(f(x)- f(x^{\oplus i}))^{2}]/4=\Sigma\)_{S∋i}\(\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\). This is squared \(\mathrm{L}_{2}\) influence, with the factor \(1/4\) fixed explicitly. The pointwise range restriction holds on the entire cube, not merely with high probability. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers; no sparsity, coefficient-size, block structure, Boolean-valued-output or quantum-realizability promise is imposed. C must be independent of n,d,f and its variance. Constant polynomials satisfy the inequality trivially with both sides zero. The one-power notation is a normalized version of a polynomial lower bound in variance and inverse degree; because \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\le 1/4\), fixed positive prefactors can be absorbed by increasing C.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal exponent C works for every admissible polynomial, or show that for every proposed C there is an admissible polynomial of positive variance for which every coordinate has influence smaller than \((\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\). Refuting one particular exponent is insufficient to refute existence of some universal exponent. An exponential-in-degree influence bound, a theorem only after randomly fixing coordinates, or a result for a restricted subclass is partial progress.

context_blocks.text: A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

Bhattacharya’s random-restriction theorem approaches the unrestricted class differently. Fix most coordinates independently to random signs and leave roughly a \(\log (d)/d\) fraction available. Under a lower bound on the original variance, a non-negligible fraction of restrictions have a polynomially influential remaining variable. The accompanying junta theorem approximates restricted functions using few coordinates. Neither assertion directly guarantees such a variable in the original, unrestricted function.

Two recent results clarify the frontier. Blanc and coauthors obtain the desired almost-everywhere classical simulation for a fixed number of quantum query rounds; their exponent depends on the number of rounds. This does not address arbitrary adaptivity or prove the full polynomial inequality. Escudero Gutiérrez, Saucedo and Palazuelos subsequently obtain an optimal root-influence inequality for completely bounded block-multilinear polynomials, improving simulation to allow nonadaptive classical queries for that setting.

The September inequality controls the sum of square roots of influences by the number of blocks times the completely bounded norm. Its extra norm hypothesis is precisely what prevents applying it to every polynomial in this card. The paper explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture. A historical general proof claim by Keller and Klein is withdrawn because of an error in a key lemma, and is recorded as a withdrawal rather than progress establishing the conjecture.

cards.title: Mansour’s conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), integer \(s\ge 2\), Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most s terms, and \(\varepsilon \in\)(\(0,1/2\)], some family \(F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) satisfies |\(F|\le \lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) and \(\sum_{S\notin F} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\le \varepsilon\)?
cards.definitions: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of literals \(x_{i}=1\) or \(x_{i}=- 1; a\) satisfied formula has value +1 and an unsatisfied formula value −1. Term widths, overlaps, and the number of occurrences of a variable are unrestricted. On the uniform probability space \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}, \chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}, \chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Parseval gives \(\sum_{S} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}=1\). Thus \(\varepsilon\)-concentration on F means that the polynomial \(g=\sum_{S\in F}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\) has \(E[(f- g)^{2}]\le \varepsilon\). The coefficients are ordinary Walsh coefficients, not a basis adapted to a different distribution. The same C must work for all \(n,s,\varepsilon\) and f. This is an existence question about the spectrum; no efficient algorithm for finding F is part of the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative resolution proves the stated bound with one universal C. A negative resolution must show that for every C some admissible \(s,n,\varepsilon\) and DNF require more than \(\lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) coefficients to leave squared Fourier mass at most \(\varepsilon\). A polynomial bound whose exponent has an unspecified dependence on \(\varepsilon\) would settle only the weaker fixed-accuracy form.

context_blocks.text: A DNF describes a function as a short list of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier expansion describes the same function through parity correlations. Mansour’s question asks whether a short description in the first language forces an approximately short description in the second. The number n of available variables may greatly exceed the number s of terms, yet the proposed number of relevant correlations depends only on s and the permitted error.

The approximation is measured in squared error under uniformly random inputs. It does not require exact agreement everywhere, and the approximating polynomial need not have Boolean outputs. Keeping the largest squared coefficients is the best approximation with that many Walsh characters. Consequently the question is a statement about how rapidly the sorted Fourier mass decays, independent of an algorithm’s ability to identify the important characters.

Sparsity and degree are different resources. A parity involving every variable has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient but has degree n. Conversely, restricting a polynomial to degree d can leave a number of possible coefficients that grows like \(n^{d}\). A theorem saying that high-degree coefficients have little total mass therefore does not by itself give the requested bound, which must avoid such dependence on the ambient dimension.

Even one wide conjunction can have many nonzero coefficients exactly. This does not contradict the conjecture: if the conjunction fixes w distinct coordinates, its satisfying event has probability \(2^{- w}\). Approximating its ±1-valued function by the constant −1 incurs squared error \(4\cdot 2^{- w}\). Rare accepting terms can therefore produce an exactly dense spectrum while contributing very little approximation error. Combining many overlapping terms is where the simple observation stops being sufficient.

There are two common strengths of the named conjecture. The weaker one allows \(s^{K(\varepsilon )}\) coefficients for an arbitrary function K of the error. The stronger one in this saved record asks for \(K(\varepsilon )=O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))\). O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explicitly distinguish these statements. The card preserves the stronger target instead of treating all polynomial concentration claims as interchangeable.

The connection to Fourier entropy explains that distinction. If the Fourier entropy were \(O(\log  s)\), Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal \(\log (1/\hat\{f\}(S)^{2})\) would capture all but \(\varepsilon\) of the mass on at most \(s^{O(1/\varepsilon )}\) coefficients. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture, combined with the influence bound for DNF, would supply such an entropy estimate. This implication gives the weaker form, but its exponent does not establish the logarithmic dependence required here.

Mansour’s classical general bound gives \(s^{O(\log  \log  s)}\) coefficients at fixed accuracy. Klivans–Lee–Wan proved polynomial concentration for a specified random-DNF model and for every fixed read number. These are substantial structural results, but randomness in the formula cannot be assumed in a worst-case statement about every DNF. Their final May 2010 revision corrects an earlier issue in the read-number argument.

Lecomte–Tan sharpen the fixed-accuracy general estimate to \(s^{O(\log  \log  k)}\), where k bounds the number of terms containing a variable. Their stronger small-read theorem gives \((s/\varepsilon )^{O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))}\) concentration for read number up to a stated roughly doubly logarithmic range. The explicit \(s/\varepsilon\) base should be retained when comparing accuracy parameters. Their work also explains how control of term covers improves Fourier estimates beyond a single global norm bound.

The learning consequences depend on access to the target. Through the agnostic-learning reduction described by Klivans–Lee–Wan, suitable sparse Fourier approximation yields efficient agnostic learning under the uniform distribution with membership queries, for fixed approximation accuracy. Such queries allow selected input points; they are stronger access than an ordinary stream of independently sampled labeled examples. This conjecture should not be advertised as automatically solving every version of passive DNF learning.

Recent neighboring results retain these distinctions. Han’s 2025 entropy estimate contains an additional sum involving individual influences, rather than the full conjectured constant times total influence. González–MacManus–Pereyra’s June 2026 revision proves FEI for further classes under structural separation conditions. Neither is a universal theorem with the strong DNF accuracy bound in the question.

Heidari–Khardon’s June 2026 revision studies generalized Fourier representations associated with Bayesian networks. Its DNF learning theorem uses membership queries and a restricted distributional model; its agnostic result concerns decision trees. These changes in basis, distribution and target class are mathematically meaningful, but they do not establish concentration of every DNF in the ordinary uniform Walsh basis used here.

cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n, M(n,d)=\max\){\(I(f): f=\operatorname{sign}(p):\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, \deg (p)\le d\), and p has no zero on the Boolean cube}, using total influence as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with \(p(x)
e 0\) at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing \(x_{i}^{2}\) to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), let \(x^{i}\) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define \(Inf_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)
e f(x^{i})]\), pointwise sensitivity \(s_{f}(x)=|\{i:f(x)
e f(x^{i})\}|\), and \(I(f)=\sum_{i} Inf_{i}(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). The constants in the requested matching asymptotic bounds must be independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing \(d=0\) adds only these trivial cases. context_blocks.text: The quantitative target is the maximum influence as a function of dimension and degree. The following history concerns the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture and the separately disproved exact-extremizer claim.

A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2D/2^{n}\). The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of \(C d\sqrt{n}\) would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with \(\sqrt{n}\); once \(d\ge \sqrt{n}\), the elementary bound \(I(f)\le n\) already suffices with \(C=1\).

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other \(n- 1\) coordinates split evenly, giving I(\(MAJ_{n}\))=\(n\cdot \operatorname{binom}(n- 1,(n- 1)/2)/2^{n- 1}\), asymptotic to \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order \(d\sqrt{n}\). Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement discussed here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives \(O(d\sqrt{n})\). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot (\log  n)^{O(d \log  d)}\cdot 2^{O(d^{2} \log  d)}\) for \(d\ge 2\). For each fixed d, this is \(\sqrt{n}\) times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area \(BSA(f)=E[\sqrt{s_{f}}(x)]\). The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from \(I(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise \(s_{f}(x)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot \sqrt{s_{f}}(x)\) yields only \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot BSA(f)\). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}; a\) graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |\(U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

cards.formal: Determine the real Grothendieck constant \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}\), defined as the least universal comparison factor between the vector and sign bilinear optima below.
cards.definitions: For positive integers m,n and a real matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define \(S(A)=\max_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^{m},\,\delta\in\{-1,1\}^{n}}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\varepsilon_i\delta_j|\) and \(V(A)=\max_{u_1,\ldots,u_m,v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^{m+n},\,\|u_i\|_2=\|v_j\|_2=1}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|\). The inner product and norm are Euclidean. Define \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}=\sup_{m,n\ge1,\,A\ne0}V(A)/S(A)\). The denominator is positive for nonzero A. Grothendieck’s inequality makes the supremum finite. The vector dimension m+n permits every possible Gram matrix of these m+n vectors; this is the unrestricted real constant, with no fixed dimension, complex vectors, computational restriction, or asymptotic input model.

cards.definitions: \(\gamma _{n}\) is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent \(N(0,1)\) coordinates. Central symmetry means \(K=- K\), with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means \(tx+(1- t)y\in K\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in [0,1]\). Write \(1_{K}\) for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is \(Inf_{v}[K]=(1/\sqrt{2}) E[1_{K}(X)(1- \langle v,X\rangle ^{2})]\). This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is \(v\perp =\{y:\langle v,y\rangle =0\}\), and \(C+\mathbb{R} v=\{y+tv:y\in C,t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection \(x- \langle v,x\rangle v\). The symmetric difference \(K\triangle \mathrm{L}\) consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on \(\gamma _{n}(K)\), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus \(\tau\) tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.

cards.definitions: A sign matrix \(A\in \{- 1,+1\}^{r\times s}\) has positive finite numbers r,s of rows and columns and has every entry specified. Its sign-rank rank±\((A)\) is the least \(D\ge 1\) for which there are unit vectors \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{r},v_{1},\ldots ,v_{s}\in \mathbb{R}\)ᴰ with \(A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle >0\) for all i,j. Equivalently it is the minimum real rank of a matrix B satisfying \(A_{ij}B_{ij}>0\) entrywise; zero entries do not realize either sign. The margin \(m(A)\) is the supremum, over such unit-vector representations in all finite dimensions D, of \(\min _{i,j} A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle\). It lies in (0,1]. In optimizing margin, the representation dimension is unrestricted; the representation of least dimension need not maximize margin. The requested d may grow arbitrarily rapidly as \(\rho\) tends to zero, but for each fixed positive \(\rho\) it must bound all matrix sizes. Equivalently, one can use a finite nondecreasing bounding function \(\eta\):[\(1,\infty\))→\(\mathbb{N}\). This uniform bounded-margin interpretation is explicitly restated in the later source’s Open Problem 1.3. Matrices with missing or promise-restricted entries are excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a finite size-independent bound \(d(\rho )\) for every positive margin threshold \(\rho\), or prove there is a fixed \(\rho >0\) and a sequence of fully specified finite sign matrices with margins at least \(\rho\) and unbounded sign-ranks. No efficient procedure for producing the low-dimensional representation is required. Unbounded sign-rank with margins tending to zero, or only for partial matrices, does not refute the statement.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\), put \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\). The Fourier coefficient is \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\), so \(f=\sum _{S\subseteq [n]}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\). The support is \(\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})=\{S:\hat\{f\}(S)\ne 0\}\), and \(k(f)=|\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})|\). It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in \(F_{2}^{n}\) and define \(r(f)=\dim _{F_{2}}\) span\(\{1_{S}:S\in \operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})\}\). The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit \(r(f_{j})=\omega (\sqrt{k}(f_{j}))\) means that for every real \(M>0\), the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on \(n_{j}\) in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that \(r(f)\le C\sqrt{k}(f)\) for every n and every such f. Since \(r(f)\le k(f)\), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.

cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know \(f\) and the finite domains. A public-coin protocol selects a deterministic binary communication tree using a finite string of independent shared fair random bits, independent of the inputs. At a node, the designated player sends one bit determined by that player’s own input, the public string and the transcript so far. At termination Bob outputs a bit determined by his input, the public string and transcript. The worst-case cost is the maximum number of communicated bits over all inputs and public strings. Local computation and the public random string are free; its finite length may depend on the protocol. There is no message to reveal the public seed, no advice depending on private inputs and no restriction to one-way communication. The complexity \(R_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum cost of a protocol whose output equals \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair. It is finite because Alice can send an encoding of her input. Protocols may depend nonuniformly on the finite function; no uniform construction from its truth table is requested. For \(f^{\otimes k}:X^k\times Y^k\to\{0,1\}^k\), Alice and Bob receive their full tuples and Bob must output \((f(x_1,y_1),\ldots,f(x_k,y_k))\). Success probability at least \(2/3\) concerns the entire vector simultaneously on every tuple pair. The inputs need not be independent draws from a distribution: the cost and error guarantees are worst-case. The protocol may communicate across coordinates in any way. The constant \(c\) must work for all domains, functions and copy counts; a different constant for each fixed function is insufficient. Zero-communication functions impose the vacuous lower bound zero.

cards.formal:
Is there a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(B\ge1\), a uniform randomized Las Vegas algorithm solves integer 3SUM with worst-case expected time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) on the word RAM defined below? An input consists of three lists \(A,B',C\), each containing at most \(n\) integers in \([-n^B,n^B]\), and the task is to decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \exists b\in B'\ \exists c\in C:\quad a+b=c.\]
The algorithm and hidden constant may depend on the fixed universe exponent \(B\); the saving \(\varepsilon\) must be independent of \(B\). This selects the polynomial-universe integer version of the source's question, with the expected-time convention used by Kopelowitz–Pettie–Porat.

The size parameter \(n\ge2\) bounds the length of each of the three lists. Repeated values are allowed and do not affect the answer; each chosen value comes from its prescribed list. A triple may contain equal numerical values from different lists. There is no single-list distinctness condition. Integers are supplied explicitly in signed binary and fit in one word of
\[w=\left\lceil(B+3)\log_2(n+1)\right\rceil\]
bits. The target equation is equality of ordinary integers, not congruence modulo the word size.

For each fixed \(B\), a uniform word-RAM algorithm has a finite program independent of \(n\) and of all list contents. Its memory cells contain \(w\)-bit words and are addressed by words. Initially only the input and its lengths are present; other cells are zero. Unit-cost instructions are reading or writing a word, copying, comparing, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts by a word-specified amount; a shift by at least \(w\) yields zero. Division by zero can be defined to return zero. The program may obtain an independent uniformly random \(w\)-bit word at unit cost. There is no arbitrary-precision unit-cost arithmetic, real-number operation, oracle or nonuniform lookup table. Any table construction, sorting and preprocessing count toward the runtime. Arithmetic on more than one word must be implemented by these instructions.

Las Vegas means that the program halts with probability one and every output produced is correct; randomization affects its runtime, not its answer. The required bound means that for each \(B\) there are \(K_B,n_B\) such that the expected number of instructions is at most \(K_B n^{2-\varepsilon}\) on every valid instance with \(n\ge n_B\). Expectation is over the program's random words, followed by a worst case over the input lists. All smaller valid instances must also be decided correctly with finite expected time. No average-case input distribution or reusable preprocessing is supplied.

An improvement by logarithmic factors alone, a fast data-structure query after expensive preprocessing, a restricted comparison-tree lower bound, or a Monte Carlo algorithm without the stipulated zero-error guarantee does not settle this selected target.

cards.title: Hitting Set conjecture
cards.area: Fine-grained complexity
cards.formal:
Is the randomized Hitting Set conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(c\ge1\) such that no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides the following problem in worst-case time \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\)? The input is two lists \(A,B\), each of \(n\) subsets of \([d]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(d=\lceil c\log_2 n\rceil\). Decide whether
\[\exists a\in A\ \forall b\in B:\quad a\cap b\ne\varnothing.\]
The chosen set must be one of the supplied sets in \(A\). This is the source's fine-grained two-list problem, not the general optimization problem of selecting a small hitting set from the universe.
cards.why: This hypothesis captures a quadratic barrier with an existential choice followed by a universal test. It supports fine-grained lower bounds for graph radius, centers and quantified geometric problems where the more familiar two-existential-quantifier orthogonal-vectors hypothesis does not directly match the task. Settling it would clarify the role of quantifier order in fine-grained complexity.

cards.definitions:
Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\). Sets are supplied explicitly as \(d\)-bit incidence vectors; lists may contain repetitions and empty sets. Equivalently, the answer is yes if some vector \(a\in A\) has integer inner product \(\sum_{j=1}^d a_j b_j>0\) with every \(b\in B\). The coordinate sum is over integers, not modulo two. The dimension constant \(c\) is fixed independently of input size.

Use a word RAM with word length \(w=\lceil4\log_2(n+2)\rceil\). Incidence vectors are packed into consecutive words, with unused bits zero. A machine has a finite program independent of \(n\), word-addressed memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, copies, comparisons, branches, arithmetic addition/subtraction/multiplication modulo \(2^w\), quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero; division by zero may return zero. A uniformly random independent \(w\)-bit word is available at unit cost. Memory initially contains only the instance; any further preprocessing or lookup-table construction is charged. There are no oracles, advice or unit-cost operations on arbitrarily long integers.

A bounded-error algorithm must output the correct yes/no answer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every valid input. Its runtime bound applies to every random tape and every input, not only in expectation. For fixed \(\varepsilon,c\), a forbidden algorithm would have constants \(K,n_0\) such that it takes at most \(Kn^{2-\varepsilon}\) instructions for every \(n\ge n_0\); the constants and program may depend on \(c,\varepsilon\). Finite smaller instances must also be decided correctly within finite time.

The order \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists c\) is essential. Refutation requires one \(\varepsilon>0\) such that for every fixed \(c\) there is an algorithm with that same exponent saving; it does not require the same program or multiplicative constant for all \(c\). Conversely, a faster algorithm at one small dimension constant does not refute the conjecture. Choosing integral \(c\) is harmless because extra zero coordinates pad smaller dimensions.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the conjecture or its negation in the stated bounded-error word-RAM model. A refutation must supply a common positive exponent saving across all fixed dimension constants. A proof conditional on another unproved hypothesis is not a proof of this conjecture. A lower bound only for deterministic algorithms, a restricted instruction set, or an isolated value of \(c\) does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: For fixed \(c\), comparing every pair of packed vectors gives an \(O(cn^2)\)-time baseline. The conjecture permits savings that vanish as dimension grows; it rules out one fixed polynomial saving valid across all dimension constants.

Orthogonal Vectors asks whether some pair has zero inner product. Here one supplied vector must have nonzero inner product with every vector on the other side. Exchanging these quantifiers changes the question, just as finding a graph center differs from finding a distant pair of vertices.

cards.title: Unconditional subexponential simulation of BPP
cards.area: Pseudorandomness and derandomization
cards.formal:
Is \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}\) unconditionally? Here the subexponential class is the intersection
\[\mathrm{SUBEXP}=\bigcap_{k\ge1}\mathrm{DTIME}\!\left(2^{n^{1/k}}\right).\]
Thus, for every language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) decidable with two-sided bounded error in randomized polynomial time, and for every integer \(k\ge1\), must there exist a deterministic algorithm deciding \(L\) on every input in time \(O(2^{n^{1/k}})\)? The algorithm and the constant in its time bound may depend on \(L,k\). The target selects the subexponential question in the source's Open Problem 3.4; its separate quasipolynomial-time question is stronger.
cards.why: This asks whether randomness can provide a much larger speedup than the usual derandomization conjectures predict, even after allowing deterministic time far beyond polynomial. An unconditional simulation would move the general worst-case upper bound into the source’s much smaller subexponential class. A counterexample would establish a major separation between randomized and deterministic computation.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. An algorithm decides \(L\) if it halts and outputs one exactly on inputs in \(L\), and zero on all other inputs. Use uniform multitape Turing machines with finite descriptions independent of input length. One transition costs one time unit. A randomized machine may additionally request independent unbiased bits, at unit cost per bit. It has no advice, oracle or preprocessing that depends on input length without being computed by the machine.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BPP}\) means that there are such a randomized machine \(M\) and constants \(a,C\ge1\) with worst-case runtime at most \(C(n+1)^a\) on every length-\(n\) input and every random tape, and with
\[x\in L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\ge2/3,\qquad x\notin L\Rightarrow\Pr[M(x)=1]\le1/3.\]
This is a class of total decision problems. The acceptance-probability gap holds on every input; it is not a promise that an external user must supply.

The notation \(L\in\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{1/k}})\) means that a deterministic machine decides \(L\) and has worst-case runtime at most \(C_k\lceil2^{n^{1/k}}\rceil\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), for some fixed \(C_k\). All finitely many smaller inputs must also be decided correctly and with termination. Requiring every integer \(k\) is equivalent to requiring time \(O(2^{n^\varepsilon})\) for every fixed real \(\varepsilon>0\). The machine is allowed to change with the exponent; an effective compiler taking \(M,k\) and producing the simulator is not an additional requirement.

This definition of SUBEXP is the source's intersection of subpower-exponential time classes. A single \(2^{o(n)}\)-time bound, such as \(2^{n/\log n}\), need not meet it. Likewise, correctness only on most inputs, or on infinitely many input lengths, is insufficient. The simulator must decide the same language exactly on all strings.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion or its negation. A positive proof must cover every BPP language and every fixed exponent \(1/k\), without a hardness assumption, oracle or advice. A negative proof must establish a language in BPP that is outside one of the deterministic time classes in the displayed intersection. A conditional simulation, a simulation for a particular randomized problem, or a heuristic correct on almost all inputs does not settle the question.

context_blocks.text: Enumerating every random tape gives a deterministic simulation in \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\) time. A polynomial-time randomized algorithm can use polynomially many random bits, so this direct simulation gives EXP rather than the displayed SUBEXP target.
If \(\mathrm{BPP}=\mathrm P\), the desired inclusion follows. The converse is not asserted: a subexponential simulator may still take much more than polynomial time.

Known hardness-versus-randomness theorems yield much stronger derandomization under suitable circuit lower-bound assumptions. For example, the Impagliazzo–Wigderson theorem derives BPP = P from exponential circuit hardness for a language computable in single-exponential time. Those hardness hypotheses are part of the conditional theorem and cannot be removed by citing it.

Fixing a good random tape separately for each length gives a nonuniform object. Uniformity requires a finite deterministic algorithm that computes its behavior; a sequence of good tapes supplied for free does not meet the target.

cards.title: Set Cover conjecture

cards.formal:
Is the Set Cover conjecture true? For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), does there exist a fixed integer \(d\ge1\) such that no uniform randomized bounded-error algorithm solves \(\le d\)-Set Cover on an \(n\)-element universe in worst-case time
\[O\!\left((2-\varepsilon)^n(n+1)^r\right)\]
for any fixed exponent \(r\)? An instance supplies a family \(\mathcal F\subseteq2^{[n]}\) with \(|S|\le d\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\), and an integer \(t\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\). The task is to decide whether some subfamily \(\mathcal H\subseteq\mathcal F\) of at most \(t\) sets satisfies \(\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal H}S=[n]\). Sets chosen for the cover may overlap. The randomized interpretation is explicit in the later primary sources.
cards.why: Set Cover is a central example of an exact algorithm whose natural dynamic-programming base remains two. The conjecture provides barriers for other exponential-time problems and is not merely a restatement of the familiar SAT hypotheses. Its incompatibility with the asymptotic rank conjecture links this algorithmic barrier to fundamental questions in algebraic complexity.

sentences: Set Cover asks whether a few supplied sets can cover a given universe.
The conjecture concerns exact algorithms when each available set has a fixed maximum size.
It says that no constant improvement over exponential base two works across all such size bounds.
